The Indian Wars. A series of armed conflicts between the United States and Native American tribes spanning from the early nineteenth century through the eighteen nineties. As American expansion moved westward, the federal government and settlers violently dispossessed indigenous peoples of their ancestral lands. These wars resulted in displacement, genocide, and the destruction of Native American societies and cultures. The Indian Wars began in earnest after the War of eighteen twelve as American settlers moved across the Mississippi River into indigenous territories, breaking treaties and igniting conflicts with established tribal nations. This expansion was driven by Manifest Destiny, the ideology that American expansion across the continent was inevitable and justified by Providence, framing indigenous peoples as obstacles to national destiny. Major conflicts included wars against the Cherokee, Creek, Seminole, Sioux, Cheyenne, Comanche, Apache, Navajo, and other tribes across multiple decades. Some lasted years and involved thousands of combatants. Legendary figures like Sitting Bull, Geronimo, and Crazy Horse led indigenous resistance against American military campaigns. Their tactical brilliance and courage earned respect even from American military opponents. President Andrew Jackson forced the Trail of Tears from eighteen thirty-eight to eighteen thirty-nine, a devastating forced removal of southeastern tribes—Cherokee, Creek, Chickasaw, Choctaw, and Seminole—to western reservations in Oklahoma, killing thousands from disease and starvation. The Indian Wars culminated in massacres like Sand Creek in eighteen sixty-four, where Colorado militia killed Cheyenne and Arapaho families, and Wounded Knee in eighteen ninety, when the U.S. Seventh Cavalry killed Lakota Sioux, symbolizing the final suppression of Native resistance. These wars resulted in the creation of the reservation system, confining surviving Native Americans to marginal lands. This policy destroyed their traditional hunting and agricultural ways of life, creating cycles of poverty and cultural disruption lasting generations.
